source.title: Decoding Dark Matter: Specialized Sparse Autoencoders for Interpreting Rare Concepts in Foundation Models
source.authors: Aashiq Muhamed; Mona T. Diab; Virginia Smith

record.tranche_reason: The study compares neuron ablation with SAE-feature circuit ablation and states that the neuron-based approach performs worse, likely because individual neurons are polysemantic. It does not audit the share of neurons with one or two jobs.
record.gate_note: The Bias in Bios comparison of neuron and SAE feature ablations bears on V5. Automated interpretability scores are for SAE features, not neuron explanations, so they do not test V6 or V7; they are recorded as related findings under fits_no_version. Results cited from other work are not recorded as study results.
record.test_reason: The study proposes Specialized SAEs and does not audit neuron jobs, score neuron explanations, or build attribution graphs from neurons. Its one neuron result is the 'Neuron skyline' baseline in a Bias in Bios debiasing task on a Pythia-70M probe classifier. That baseline mean-ablates up to 200 neurons and reports classifier accuracy. This measures how well neuron ablation edits a spurious signal compared with SAE-feature ablation. It does not measure whether a large model's own neurons explain its behaviour without a replacement model, so it does not test V5. The authors' attribution of the gap to polysemantic neurons is cited from Marks et al., not tested. The automated-interpretability F1 scores concern SAE features, not neurons, so V6 and V7 are not tested either. The neuron-versus-SAE editing result is recorded under fits_no_version.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct. The authors conclude that SSAEs (dense retrieval plus finetuning, optionally TERM) capture more tail concepts than general SAEs. They report a 12.5-point worst-group gain on Bias in Bios (88.5 vs 76.0), and say TERM-trained SSAEs give more predictive explanations. The statement that neuron skyline underperforms 'likely due to' neuron polysemanticity is an aside credited to Marks et al. (2024), not a conclusion the study tests.
record.recipe_differences: The study uses SAE feature circuits and neuron ablation for a Bias in Bios classifier, plus automated scoring of SAE-feature explanations. It does not use the original Qwen3 neuron-pole audit or audit neuron-job shares.
record.method_sensitivity: In the Bias in Bios results, compressed versus uncompressed SAE width and whether the linear probe is retrained change outcomes. The paper also reports automated interpretability results varying SAE training strategy (OWT, dense retrieval, dense retrieval with tilt).

fits_no_version.finding: In a Pythia-70M Bias in Bios probe classifier, mean-ablating up to 200 neurons (Neuron skyline) raised worst-group accuracy from 24.4 to 41.5. SAE-feature SHIFT reached 76.0 (GSAE) and 88.5 (SSAE). Neuron ablation also left gender accuracy higher (73.2 vs 54.0 and 53.4).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: For removing a spurious signal by ablation in a small LM classifier, neuron units are less effective edit targets than SAE features.

fits_no_version.finding: SAE-feature explanations from TERM-trained SSAEs get higher sequence-level prediction F1 than OWT-baseline and ERM-trained SSAE explanations on Physics arXiv (Gemma-2b). These are figure-only results.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Explanation predictiveness of SAE features depends on the SAE training objective.

record.code_released: All code, experiments, and ablations are stated to be publicly released upon acceptance; no URL is stated.
record.peer_reviewed: North American Chapter of the Association for Computational Linguistics
record.problems: The neuron-versus-SAE comparison is limited to a Pythia-70M linear classifier on Bias in Bios. Table 1 reports no uncertainty estimates. Automated interpretability scores are shown only in a figure, with no numeric F1 values stated in the text.
record.rows_left_out: The CBP and Oracle rows in Table 1 are omitted because they are not neuron or SAE-feature circuit-unit comparisons for V5. The Original classifier is used as the stated baseline for the intervention rows rather than recorded as a separate operation.

untested.parts: No neuron-pole audit or share of one-job, two-job or unexplained neurons.
No neuron interpretability shares across models or scales.
No InceptionV1 or canonical polysemantic neuron analysis.
No neuron interpretability share versus architecture or tools.
No attribution graphs built from neurons in a large model. The neuron-ablation debiasing baseline in Pythia-70M does not measure explanatory sufficiency.
No test of neuron explanations from activating examples; explanations are of SAE features.
No simulation-based scoring of neuron explanations; F1 scores are for SAE features and are shown only in a figure.

record.verdict_notes: The reader labeled V5 limits_scope, but the neuron skyline is a debiasing baseline in a 70M probe, not an attribution-graph explanation in a large model, so no verdict is given. The neuron-baseline numbers can be read from Table 1. The paper is not one of the original sources. Its Interpreter prompt calls SAE features 'neurons', which might mislead a reader into linking the explanation boxes to V6 or V7; they describe SAE features.

versions.untested_parts: The share of neuron poles with one job, two related jobs, or not-yet-understood jobs.
Interpretable-neuron shares across models, architectures, and scales.
The InceptionV1 cat-and-car example, pose, or recursive generalization.
Neuron interpretability shares across architectures, tools, or vision-model sizes.

The study tests neuron versus SAE-feature ablation in a Pythia-70M classifier, not attribution graphs built from a large model’s own neurons generally. It does not test whether graphs explain behavior without a trained replacement model and reconstruction error.
The automated explanation evaluation uses SAE features, not neuron explanations; it does not directly test explanations of neuron-activating examples.
The automated explanation evaluation uses SAE features, not neurons, and does not report the share of neurons attaining good scores.

relation.reason: Mentions neuron polysemanticity and superposition in passing as background and as an aside. It does not test or use the claim. The reader's tests/T5 call is not supported.

tranche.reason: Proposes Specialized SAEs. Neuron skyline is only a debiasing baseline on a Pythia-70M probe, and the polysemanticity remark cites Marks et al. without measuring it. Nothing tests neuron cleanliness.

source_check.notes: All 20 rows match the Table 1 cells (Prof, Gen, Worst) and the Figure 8 text. Neuron skyline mean-ablates 1-200 neurons in a 70M probe setup and measures debiasing, not explanation. The Figure 8 F1 scores rate SAE features, not neurons, so they do not bear on V7. No verdicts are listed and none are warranted.

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: Pythia-70M classifier on the Bias in Bios balanced set, without probe retraining
reader_labels.reason: Neuron skyline improves the measures over Original but is substantially below SAE-feature SHIFT on profession and worst-group accuracy, and leaves higher gender accuracy (bib-neuron-prof, bib-neuron-gender, bib-neuron-worst; comparisons bib-gsae-prof, bib-gsae-gender, bib-gsae-worst, bib-ssae-prof, bib-ssae-gender, bib-ssae-worst). This is a limited classifier case, not a direct test of attribution graphs generally.
